A previously healthy 29-year-old man presents with a two-day history of a mild febrile illness, followed by rapidly progressive altered mental status and generalized seizures. On arrival he is encephalopathic with a depressed level of consciousness.
Which of the following diagnoses best explains the imaging findings?
Classically pediatric; adult cases are rare (adult IAE incidence ~0.19–0.21 per million/
Mortality is higher in adults (case fatality up to 17–20% in those ≥40
Rapid neurologic deterioration days after an influenza respiratory prodrome: fever, altered mental status/reduced consciousness progressing to coma, seizures, delirium.
Virus rarely isolated from CSF; often elevated CSF protein .
Thalamus always affected +/- necrosis and hemorrhage
Diffusion restriction and T2 hyperintensity are often seen with variable degrees of hemorrhage and enhancement
May involve brainstem, cerebellum, corpus callosum, and cerebral white matter; MR spectroscopy may show elevated lactate .
Poor overall; brainstem involvement and hemorrhage predict worse outcomes.
Only ~30–50% of IAE recover without sequelae.
: A rare variant where in a single dominant thalamoperforating artery supplies bilateral medial thalami and rostral midbrain.
Symmetric FLAIR hyperintensities with restricted diffusion involving paramedian thalami with or without rostral midbrain
V sign: V shaped hyperintensity on axial FLAIR and DWI along pial surface of midbrain adjacent to the interpeduncular fossa

A 62-year-old man underwent multilevel ACDF (C3–C7) for degenerative cervical stenosis. He awoke at his neurologic baseline. One day postoperatively, he developed progressive weakness, deteriorating to quadriplegia.
What is the leading proposed mechanism for the MRI findings?
Venous congestion due to impaired venous outflow

: Coined by Chin et al. (2013): unexplained incomplete paralysis after cervical decompression with high intramedullary T2 signal and no residual stenosis/compressive element.  Diagnosis of exclusion — a "post-decompression" reperfusion phenomenon, not mechanical injury or hematoma.

: Chronically compressed cord is hypoperfused; abrupt decompression → sudden reperfusion → ischemia–reperfusion injury, oxygen-derived free radicals, disruption of blood–spinal cord barrier, and cord edema.
: after cervical decompression ~2–5.7%; up to 14.5% after thoracic decompressive laminectomy.
: Advanced age, long-segment/extensive surgery, posterior approach, and OPLL.
Sagittal T2/STIR intramedullary hyperintensity, mean span ~4 levels (range 1–11); may persist >6 weeks, then largely resolve to subtle gliosis without cord atrophy.
Typically NO true DWI restriction (helps distinguish from cord infarction).
Axial "snake-eyes"/bilateral symmetric anterior ovoid foci described.
No compressive hematoma or residual stenosis — key differentiator.
: New deficit from monoparesis to quadriplegia; onset immediate to within days.
: 25% never recover; preoperative neurologic status is the only factor predicting final outcome.
Elderly patient ~6 hours following right carotid endarterectomy developed left-sided weakness.
A 23-year-old man presents with a progressively worsening headache. An MRI performed at an OSH reportedly demonstrated a lesion suggestive of a colloid cyst.
Which of the following diagnoses best explains the imaging findings?
Most common pediatric suprasellar tumor; ~5–11% of pediatric intracranial tumors .
Multilobulated mixed cystic-solid mass with finger-like projections.
Cyst = often T1-hyperintense, variable T2; fluid-fluid levels/sediment can be seen.
Nodular enhancement of solid parts; rim enhancement of cysts.
/3rd ventricle), optic chiasm and hypothalamic involvement — drives surgical approach and morbidity.
A 40-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with headache and confusion.
Which of the following diagnoses best explains the imaging findings?
Origin: Arises from mesenchymal cells / embryonic cartilaginous rests at skull base synchondroses
Lateral in ~85% vs ~10% for chordoma, though midline cases occur (~15%).
CT: lytic bone destruction with chondroid matrix mineralization — "ring-and-arc" calcification.
MRI: T1 hypo-/isointense, markedly T2 hyperintense, avid heterogeneous ("arabesque"/honeycomb) enhancement.
DWI/ADC: high ADC (often ≥1750 × 10⁻⁶ mm²/s) is a distinguishing feature from chordoma (low ADC);
Favorable outcome: 5-yr OS ~80–90%, better than chordoma.
Malignant tumor arising from remnants of the primitive notochord.
Typically occurs in the midline, most commonly in the sacrum or clivus.
Can arise anywhere along the course of the primitive notochord.
Slow-growing tumor that often presents at a large size.
Locally invasive, but distant metastases are uncommon.
Recurrence is common, often occurring along the operative tract.
T2-weighted MRI: Typically demonstrates high signal intensity due to its high fluid content.-
Internal septations: Low-signal-intensity septations are commonly seen on T2-weighted images.-
Vascular relationships: commonly displace or partially encase adjacent arteries (narrowing is rare, unlike in meningiomas).
Treatment typically involves surgical excision followed by radiation therapy.
Local recurrence is common despite treatment.
A 66-year-old woman presents with progressive spasticity and weakness of the left upper extremity. She has been undergoing physiotherapy for the past 3 years without significant clinical improvement.
Which of the following diagnoses best explains the imaging and clinical findings?
Ischemic insult and subsequent Wallerian degeneration
: Asymmetric rigidity, bradykinesia, limb apraxia, dystonia, alien limb phenomenon, imbalance, and cognitive decline.
Asymmetric posterior frontal + superior parietal cortical atrophy contralateral to the more affected limb.
White-matter loss in body of corpus callosum, premotor/motor subcortical WM.
Midbrain and superior cerebellar peduncles spared (contrast with PSP).
: Predominant frontal atrophy with behavioral changes.
Parkinson disease (PD): Typically lacks marked cortical atrophy.
Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP): Predominant midbrain atrophy.
A 75-year-old woman with a known occipital meningioma under surveillance presents with a 1-year history of progressive imbalance and recurrent falls.
Which of the following diagnoses best explains the imaging and clinical findings?
Cognitive decline, abnormal eye movements (supranuclear vertical gaze palsy), postural instability and falls, as well as Parkinsonian features and speech disturbances
Wide range of clinical variants, overlap with many other
Midbrain to pons ratio: <0.52, midbrain diameter <9.35 mm
MSA: predominantly pontine atrophy, hot cross bun
A 49-year-old woman with a history of sickle cell disease (SCD) presents to the emergency department with painful left-sided ophthalmoplegia
Which of the following diagnoses best explains the imaging and clinical findings?
: Rare; incidence approximately 4–5 cases per million.
Spread from facial, paranasal sinus, or dental infections.
Trauma, hypercoagulable states (malignancy, pregnancy, thrombophilia), and inflammatory disorders (SLE,
: Painful ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, fever, headache, and occasionally seizures.
Heterogeneous enhancement and possible filling defect.
Associated superior ophthalmic vein (SOV) enlargement and thrombosis, sometimes with surrounding inflammatory changes.
Prominent cavernous sinus enhancement and dilated SOV; SOV thrombosis is not typical.
Consider with a known primary malignancy, infiltrative enhancement, or cranial neuropathies.
–Hunt syndrome; imaging may overlap with thrombosis.
Meningioma, cavernous venous malformation, and schwannoma; typically show a mass-like pattern of enhancement and may be incidental.

A 34-year-old woman presents with transient right-sided upper and lower limb weakness and slurred speech lasting approximately 3 hours, with complete resolution. She reports prior similar episodes and has a history of scalp alopecia.
Which of the following diagnoses best explains the imaging and clinical findings?
Cerebral Autosomal Recessive Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy
: Autosomal recessive; caused by HTRA1 mutations.
: Early-onset cognitive decline, gait disturbance, spasticity, and recurrent subcortical strokes.
: Extensive, symmetric periventricular and deep white-matter hyperintensities; lacunar infarcts; white-matter atrophy.
: Typically presents in young adulthood, without a dominant family history.

runs.t: A 23-year-old man with sickle cell disease presents with a sudden decrease in level of consciousness.
: Neurological manifestation of fat embolism syndrome caused by bone marrow necrosis.
-occlusion → bone marrow necrosis → release of marrow fat into circulation → cerebral microvascular injury.
: Sudden altered mental status, reduced level of consciousness, seizures, and potentially coma.
DWI: Multiple punctate foci of restricted diffusion (starfield pattern)
SWI/GRE: Numerous punctate microhemorrhages (walnut kernel pattern).
May involve the cerebral white matter, corpus callosum, deep gray nuclei, and cerebellum.
Can occur spontaneously in SCD without preceding trauma.

) presents with a 2-day history of headache.
Non-neoplastic production of blood cells outside the bone marrow, involving erythroid, myeloid, and megakaryocytic lineages.
Compensatory response to chronic anemia, ineffective erythropoiesis, or marrow replacement.
Common sites: Liver, spleen, lymph nodes, and paravertebral tissues.
Often incidental; may cause headache, nasal obstruction, or sinusitis-like symptoms.
Skull-base extension may cause cranial neuropathies or visual impairment due to compression.
CT: Expansile sinus mass, loss of aeration, and possible internal trabecular or calcific changes; bone remodeling may be present.
MRI: Variable T1/T2 signal and enhancement, depending on hematopoietic activity, fat content, and iron deposition.
Nuclear medicine: Tc-99m sulfur colloid scintigraphy may help confirm hematopoietic tissue in selected cases.
Chordoma, fibrous dysplasia, meningioma, metastasis, plasmacytoma, dermoid, inverted papilloma, and fungal sinusitis.

runs.t: Papillary Carcinoma in Thyroglossal Duct Cyst
Rare complication of a thyroglossal duct cyst; papillary thyroid carcinoma is the predominant histological subtype.
Typically presents in adults as a midline neck mass.
Location: Midline or paramedian cystic lesion along the embryological course of the thyroglossal duct, commonly near the hyoid bone.
: Well-defined cystic lesion with an enhancing mural nodule or solid component; internal calcifications may be present.
: Predominantly cystic lesion with an enhancing mural nodule or solid component. Signal intensity of the cystic contents varies with proteinaceous material or hemorrhage.
